summary:
xikomu uses NASA Earth observation data to give Mozambican farmers district-level advice on what to sow and when.

NASA GLDAS (Global Land Data Assimilation System): Our core dataset. We use monthly precipitation from 2000 to 2026 for all 159 districts, about 50,000 records. It lets us say things like "in 20 of 26 years the rain was enough for this crop". It also gives us the rain-onset month, the best and worst past seasons, and the risk months for each crop until harvest. It is the training data for our seasonal outlook model, which predicts dry, normal or wet seasons.

NASA POWER: We use temperature climatology for each district. We compare it with each crop's ideal temperature range when we calculate its compatibility score.

Both sources cover the whole country, so no ground sensors are needed. This matters in a region with few weather stations and no measured yield records.

We combine this NASA data with open sources: SoilGrids for soil, Open-Meteo for the 16-day forecast, NOAA's El Niño index, and Esri land cover. The result is a compatibility score for each crop and a comparison of three rotations. It is presented in plain language in English, Portuguese and Changana.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

xikomu is a free web app that helps smallholder farmers in Mozambique decide what to sow, when, and in which rotation. It works at the level of the district, for 159 districts.

The farmer picks their district and the date they plan to sow.

The app pulls together NASA and open data for that place:

NASA GLDAS: monthly rainfall for every district, 2000–2026.

NASA POWER: temperature climatology.

SoilGrids: soil pH and texture.

Open-Meteo: a 16-day weather forecast.

NOAA ONI: the El Niño index.

Esri Sentinel-2: 2025 land cover.

It scores each crop from 0 to 100% for that district and date. The score compares rain over the crop's growing cycle, temperature, pH and soil texture with the crop's ideal ranges. It covers cereals, legumes, roots, 8 vegetables and perennials such as sugarcane, banana and lychee.

It turns 26 years of rainfall into plain statements, for example "In 20 of 26 years the rain was enough for this crop." It also shows the best and worst past seasons.

A trained model, a calibrated logistic regression on El Niño, gives a seasonal outlook of dry, normal or wet. It is used only where it beat the historical baseline (south and centre, October–January sowing).

For each crop it shows the risk periods to watch until harvest: the 16-day forecast first, then how often past years had too much or too little rain in each month.

It compares three crop rotations (for example legume-cereal), with a bonus for legumes and variety and a penalty for monocultures.

A built-in AI assistant, restricted to the district's analysis, answers farmers' questions.

The interface is in English, Portuguese and Changana (local language).


What benefits does it have?

  • Better sowing decisions. Farmers see how reliable a crop has been in their district, not just a single forecast.
  • Honest uncertainty. Each result says how many years it is based on. The model is used only where validation showed it helps.
  • Rotation planning. It helps with soil health and resilience, and puts legumes into the plan.
  • Accessible. It is free, needs no account, and works in local languages. Results are written in plain sentences instead of technical charts.
  • Built on open NASA data that is available for the whole country, so it needs no ground sensors.
What is the intended impact of the project?
  • Fewer failed plantings and lower losses from drought or flooding, especially for smallholders who rely on rain-fed farming.
  • More stable food security and household income in rural Mozambique.
  • A shift from planting "as we always did" to planting based on evidence. This supports climate adaptation as rainfall becomes less predictable.
  • A scalable base. The same method works for any country with NASA Earth observation coverage. Extension officers and agricultural technicians can also use it as a support tool.

How is your project creative?

  • It turns NASA satellite and model data into farmer language. "In 20 of 26 years the rain was enough" is something a farmer can judge for themselves.
  • It looks at the whole crop cycle, not just sowing day. It flags the specific months to watch until harvest.
  • It compares rotations instead of single crops. It also keeps perennial crops in a separate list, so the scoring stays fair.
  • It uses AI under constraints. The assistant can only answer from the district's data, so it doesn't invent advice.
  • It supports Changana, a local language, which most agri-tech tools ignore.
  • Crops, pests and rotations live in a database, so agronomists can update them without touching code.

What factors did your team consider?

- Data availability

- Climate variability (El Niño)

- Rainfall timing

- Soil conditions

- Crop biology

- Rotation and soil health

- Farmer needs

- Language and access

- Uncertainty and limits

- Transparency and trust

- Different crop types
